# Nopal

> Cross-platform UI framework for OCaml using MVU (Model-View-Update) architecture. Build local-first applications targeting desktop, mobile, and web from a single OCaml codebase.

Nopal compiles to JavaScript via js_of_ocaml for web and Tauri webview targets. Desktop and mobile are served via Tauri. The framework is not a React-style VDOM framework — it uses a pure description type (`Element.t`) that renderers interpret directly.

Homepage: nopal.run

## Architecture

Every concern is a separate opam package with strict one-way dependency flow:

```
nopal_mvu       ← MVU core (Cmd, Sub, App, Task, Key_chord, Clipboard) — depends on nopal_element for the types Cmd/Sub/App carry (Scroll_delta.t, Viewport.t, Element.t); no platform deps
nopal_element   ← Element.t DSL — no platform deps
nopal_style     ← Typed layout/paint — no platform deps
nopal_storage   ← Backend-agnostic async key-value storage contract (module type S, In_memory, With_codec) — no platform deps
nopal_platform  ← Type-safe bidirectional routing + platform-capability signatures (Platform.NAV, Platform.S) — depends on nopal_storage, and on nopal_element for Router.destination's Link.destination; no platform deps (renamed from nopal_router)
nopal_scene     ← Pure scene types (Color, Paint, Transform, Path segments, Scene, Graphic_name) — no platform deps
nopal_draw      ← 2D drawing DSL (Scale, the shared arc sweep resolver Arc, and higher-level Path algorithms) — depends on nopal_scene
nopal_svg       ← Pure SVG 1.1 string renderer for nopal_scene — depends on nopal_scene and nopal_draw; no platform deps
nopal_charts    ← Composable interactive charts (Bar, Line, Area, Pie, Scatter, Sparkline,
                   Heat_map, Trading.Candlestick, Trading.Drawdown, Chart_pane,
                   Color_scale, Domain_window, Viewport, Downsample, Snap)
nopal_http      ← Pure HTTP types + backend abstraction — no platform deps
nopal_navigation ← Nav_stack: pure stack-based navigation state (non-empty, total pop) — no platform deps
nopal_image     ← Validated RGBA Buffer, perceptual Luma, Sharpness metric, capture Config, Processing + Preview + Retention seams — depends on nopal_mvu (Task/Cmd types); no platform deps
nopal_ui        ← High-level UI components (Bottom_tabs, Button, Checkbox, Data_table, Modal, Navigation_bar, Radio_group, Select_input, Slug, Text_input, Text_node, Toast) — no platform deps
nopal_runtime   ← Lwd reactive integration + MVU loop; Telemetry (E2E event log)
nopal_test      ← Pure OCaml test renderer + Telemetry_test harness — no js_of_ocaml
nopal_web       ← js_of_ocaml + Brr DOM renderer (only browser-dependent package)
nopal_http_web  ← Browser Fetch API backend for nopal_http — depends on nopal_blob_web (multipart file parts); js_of_ocaml + Brr, never nopal_web/nopal_runtime/lwd
nopal_blob_web  ← Session-local handle ⇄ Brr.Blob.t registry + displayable object URLs, reachable from any _web backend — js_of_ocaml + Brr
nopal_image_web ← Browser canvas pipeline implementing Nopal_image.Processing, and the browser side of Nopal_image.Preview and Nopal_image.Retention — depends on nopal_image + nopal_mvu + nopal_blob_web; js_of_ocaml + Brr, never nopal_web/nopal_runtime/lwd
nopal_storage_web   ← IndexedDB backend implementing Nopal_storage.S — js_of_ocaml + Brr
nopal_storage_tauri ← Filesystem (tauri-plugin-fs) backend implementing Nopal_storage.S — js_of_ocaml + Brr
nopal_tauri     ← Tauri desktop/mobile bindings — depends on nopal_mvu (for Task.t), nopal_platform (for Platform.S); no UI package.
                   Its sub-library nopal_tauri.mount (module Nopal_tauri_mount) is the Tauri mount entry point and
                   depends on nopal_web, so the nopal_tauri opam package now depends on nopal_web
nopal_telemetry_wire ← Shared telemetry event ⇄ JS wire codec for nopal_web + nopal_tauri — js_of_ocaml + Brr
```

Critical boundary: `nopal_element`, `nopal_style`, `nopal_test`, `nopal_platform`, `nopal_storage`, `nopal_image` must compile on native OCaml without js_of_ocaml. Application view code never imports `nopal_web` or `Brr`.

## Quick Start

### Setup

```bash
opam install . --deps-only --with-test
just build    # opam exec -- dune build
just test     # opam exec -- dune runtest
just          # build + test + fmt + lint (run before every commit)
```

### Minimal Counter App

**counter.ml** — Pure model, update, and view:

```ocaml
open Nopal_element
open Nopal_style

type model = { count : int }
type msg = Increment | Decrement | Reset

let init () = ({ count = 0 }, Nopal_mvu.Cmd.none)

let update model = function
  | Increment -> ({ count = model.count + 1 }, Nopal_mvu.Cmd.none)
  | Decrement -> ({ count = max 0 (model.count - 1) }, Nopal_mvu.Cmd.none)
  | Reset -> ({ count = 0 }, Nopal_mvu.Cmd.none)

let button_style =
  Style.default
  |> Style.with_layout (fun l ->
       { l with width = Some (Fixed 64.0) } |> Style.padding 8.0 16.0 8.0 16.0)

let view model =
  column
    ~style:
      (Style.default
      |> Style.with_layout (fun l ->
           { l with cross_align = Some Center; gap = Some 8.0 } |> Style.padding_all 16.0))
    [
      text (string_of_int model.count);
      button ~style:button_style ~on_click:Increment (text "+");
      button ~style:button_style ~on_click:Decrement (text "-");
      button ~style:button_style ~on_click:Reset (text "Reset");
    ]

let subscriptions _model = Nopal_mvu.Sub.none
```

**main.ml** — Web mounting (the only file that touches browser APIs):

```ocaml
let () =
  let open Brr in
  let target =
    match Document.find_el_by_id G.document (Jstr.v "app") with
    | Some el -> el
    | None ->
        let body = Document.body G.document in
        let div = El.div [] in
        El.append_children body [ div ];
        div
  in
  Nopal_web.mount
    (module Counter : Nopal_mvu.App.S
      with type model = Counter.model
       and type msg = Counter.msg)
    target
```

## Core API Reference

### App Module (`nopal_mvu`)

Every Nopal application implements this signature:

```ocaml
module type App.S = sig
  type model
  type msg
  val init          : unit -> model * msg Cmd.t
  val update        : model -> msg -> model * msg Cmd.t
  val view          : model -> msg Element.t
  val subscriptions : model -> msg Sub.t
end
```

### Commands (`Cmd.t`)

Pure descriptions of side effects — never execute directly. The runtime interprets them.

```ocaml
Cmd.none                                      (* no effect *)
Cmd.batch : 'msg Cmd.t list -> 'msg Cmd.t     (* combine multiple commands *)
  (* Children are interpreted in list order, and flattening a nested batch
     preserves that order, so an effect that has to be started before another —
     a stored image released before something asks after it again — goes ahead
     of it in the list. Order of interpretation is not order of completion: an
     async effect started first may finish last. *)
Cmd.perform : (('msg -> unit) -> unit) -> 'msg Cmd.t  (* general effect — zero, one, or many dispatches *)
Cmd.task : 'msg Task.t -> 'msg Cmd.t                  (* async task effect *)
Cmd.after : int -> 'msg -> 'msg Cmd.t         (* delay message by N ms *)
Cmd.focus : string -> 'msg Cmd.t              (* request focus on element by id *)
  (* Outbound only, and it carries no message. The inbound direction — a model
     learning that focus arrived or left — is Element.box's ~on_focus/~on_blur
     and Element.input's ~on_focus. *)
Cmd.scroll_by : string -> Nopal_element.Scroll_delta.t -> 'msg Cmd.t
  (* Move the scroll container carrying that DOM id by a signed multiple of the
     container's own visible height — the id is the one passed as an [attrs]
     pair to Element.scroll. One-shot: acted on once and never replayed, so two
     identical requests move the container twice and several in one batch
     compose rather than overwrite. An id naming nothing, an id naming
     something that cannot scroll, and a backend that renders no elements are
     all the same no-op, and none of them is an error. Carries no message. *)
Cmd.write_clipboard :
  string -> on_result:((unit, Clipboard.error) result -> 'msg) -> 'msg Cmd.t
  (* Place a string on the system clipboard; on_result receives the outcome,
     exactly once. Issue it from the update that handles the click. See
     Clipboard below. *)
Cmd.map : ('a -> 'b) -> 'a Cmd.t -> 'b Cmd.t  (* transform message type *)
```

`Cmd.scroll_by` and `Element.scroll`'s `?reveal` both write one container's
scroll offset, and a frame that carries both applies them in a fixed order:
**reveal first, relative scroll second, focus last**. The imperative request
wins over the derived one because the application issued it in that update.
Focus is last and takes no `preventScroll`, so batching `Cmd.focus` on an
off-screen target with a `Cmd.scroll_by` lands at focus's position, not the
scroll's.

#### Focus

Focus has two directions and they are different mechanisms; reaching for the
wrong one is the usual reason an application concludes the framework cannot do
this.

**To move focus** — a command, from `update`:

```ocaml
| Opened -> ({ model with open_ = true }, Cmd.focus "email")
```

`Cmd.focus id` names an element by its DOM id, which is a pair the view put in
`~attrs`:

```ocaml
Element.input ~attrs:[ ("id", "email") ] ~on_change:Typed model.email
```

It carries no message and reports no outcome. An id naming nothing is a no-op,
not an error. Because the request is applied after the frame's DOM patch, an
element created in the same update as the `Cmd.focus` that targets it is
focusable — the element exists by the time the request drains. Within one frame
the order is **reveal first, relative scroll second, focus last** (above), so a
`Cmd.focus` batched with a `Cmd.scroll_by` lands at focus's position.

**To learn that focus moved** — a handler, into `update`:

```ocaml
Element.input ~on_focus:Focused ~on_blur:Blurred model.value
Element.box ~focusable:true ~on_focus:Entered ~on_blur:Left [ ... ]
```

`Element.input` takes `?on_focus`/`?on_blur`; `Element.box` takes both plus
`?focusable`, and its edges are scoped to the whole subtree — a box reports
focus arriving anywhere inside it and leaving all of it, so a field group can
track "is anything in me focused" without per-field wiring. `?focusable` places
the container in the platform's natural tab order.

There is no `autofocus` field and none is needed: `Cmd.focus` from `init`'s
command focuses on first render, which is also the version an application can
make conditional.

#### Clipboard

Writing plain text to the system clipboard is a command, so `update` stays pure
and the application imports no backend. The outcome comes back as one message:

```ocaml
type msg = Copy_clicked | Copied of (unit, Nopal_mvu.Clipboard.error) result

| Copy_clicked ->
    (model, Cmd.write_clipboard model.api_key ~on_result:(fun r -> Copied r))
| Copied (Ok ()) -> ({ model with note = "Copied" }, Cmd.none)
| Copied (Error Nopal_mvu.Clipboard.Not_permitted) -> ...  (* refused *)
| Copied (Error Nopal_mvu.Clipboard.Unavailable) -> ...    (* no clipboard *)
| Copied (Error (Nopal_mvu.Clipboard.Failed reason)) -> ...
```

Every write resolves exactly once — a rejected, thrown or absent platform API
is an `Error`, never only a console line. The reason is a variant; match it,
do not parse a message:

```ocaml
type Nopal_mvu.Clipboard.error =
  | Not_permitted     (* the platform refused the write *)
  | Unavailable       (* there is no clipboard to write to *)
  | Failed of string  (* anything else: the platform's reason, never the text *)
```

| Situation | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Browser: `navigator.clipboard` or `writeText` absent (not a secure context — only `https` pages and `localhost` are — or an old browser) | `Error Unavailable` |
| Browser: `writeText` rejects with `NotAllowedError` (permission denied, or no user activation) | `Error Not_permitted` |
| Tauri: the ACL refuses the command (permission not granted, or plugin not registered — both are setup mistakes with the same fix) | `Error Not_permitted` |
| A runtime created with no clipboard handler (`Runtime.create`'s default) | `Error Unavailable` |
| Anything else (another rejection, a throw, `Nopal_tauri.Clipboard.write` outside Tauri) | `Error (Failed reason)` |

**Issue the write from the `update` that handles the click.** Browsers allow a
clipboard write only within the user activation of a gesture. The runtime
interprets a command on the same call stack as the click that produced it, and
the web backend calls `writeText` synchronously there, so a write returned from
that `update` runs inside the window. A write returned from a message that
arrives later — a `Task` completion, a `Cmd.after`, an HTTP response — may be
refused as `Not_permitted`, depending on the browser. Chromium with the
`clipboard-write` permission granted accepts a write with no gesture at all
(observed in Playwright's Chromium 145), so a Chromium-only test cannot show a
write that left the window; do not take that as portable. When the text comes
from a request, fetch it first and copy on the user's next click.

**Nopal never logs the copied text, and it does not redact your state.**
`Cmd.describe` names the command `"write_clipboard"` and never its text, so the
telemetry `Command` event carries no text, and a `Failed` reason never contains
it. The telemetry log records messages and the model through the application's
own `serialize_msg` and `serialize_model` (passed to
`Nopal_web.mount_with_telemetry` or `Runtime.create_with_telemetry`), so an
application copying a secret — an API key, a token — keeps it out of those
serialisers and out of anything else it logs. Both default to `"<opaque>"`.

**Testing.** No test backend has a clipboard: the `Telemetry_test` harness
records the `Command "write_clipboard"` event and resolves the write
`Error Unavailable`, the runtime default. Assert
on the request structurally, then feed the outcome you want through `update`:

```ocaml
Cmd.extract_clipboard_writes :
  'msg Cmd.t -> (string * ((unit, Clipboard.error) result -> 'msg)) list
(* Every write in the command tree, recursing into batch, in issue order: its
   text and the callback that turns an outcome into a message. *)

let model, cmd = App.update model Copy_clicked in
match Cmd.extract_clipboard_writes cmd with
| [ (text, on_result) ] ->
    (* text is the key; now drive the refusal branch *)
    let model, _ =
      App.update model (on_result (Error Nopal_mvu.Clipboard.Not_permitted))
    in ...
| _ -> Alcotest.fail "expected exactly one clipboard write"
```

**Backends.** `Nopal_web.mount` and `mount_with_telemetry` write with the
browser's asynchronous Clipboard API unless given `?write_clipboard`. A Tauri
app mounts through `Nopal_tauri_mount` (library `nopal_tauri.mount`), which
passes `Nopal_tauri.Clipboard.write` there; it writes through the official
`tauri-plugin-clipboard-manager`. `Nopal_web.mount` on a Tauri page without
`~open_external` refuses to mount (see Tauri Bindings → Links and the Tauri
mount), so a Tauri app no longer selects the clipboard handler itself. The
desktop manual check is pending (not yet run) and mobile — plain text only, per
the plugin's documentation — is not verified by Nopal:

```ocaml
(* main.ml — the one place that knows the platform. Nopal ships no Tauri
   probe; this is the kitchen sink's own check. *)
let has_tauri () =
  not (Jv.is_undefined (Jv.get Jv.global "__TAURI_INTERNALS__"))

let () =
  if has_tauri () then ignore (Nopal_tauri_mount.mount (module App) root)
  else ignore (Nopal_web.mount (module App) root)
```

The Tauri host needs three edits:

```toml
# src-tauri/Cargo.toml, under [dependencies]
tauri-plugin-clipboard-manager = "2"
```

```rust
// src-tauri/src/lib.rs, on the tauri::Builder chain
.plugin(tauri_plugin_clipboard_manager::init())
```

```json
// src-tauri/capabilities/default.json, in the "permissions" list
"clipboard-manager:allow-write-text",
```

Grant `clipboard-manager:allow-write-text` and nothing else.
`clipboard-manager:allow-read-text` lets the webview read the clipboard, which
copying never needs. `clipboard-manager:default` is not a shortcut: in
`tauri-plugin-clipboard-manager` 2.3.3 its permission list is empty, so it
grants no clipboard command at all and the write is refused as `Not_permitted`.

**Recheck on a `tauri` version bump.** `Nopal_tauri.Clipboard` recognises an
access-control refusal by the exact words of the `tauri` version named in `backends/nopal_tauri/clipboard.ml`: the release
build's `Command plugin:clipboard-manager|write_text not allowed by ACL`, and
the debug build's messages beginning `clipboard-manager.write_text not allowed`
or `clipboard-manager.write_text explicitly denied`. When the locked `tauri`
version changes, re-read the ACL check in `src/webview/mod.rs` and
`resolve_access_message` in `src/ipc/authority.rs`, and update the decoder in
`backends/nopal_tauri/clipboard.ml` if either is reworded. Until then a
reworded refusal arrives as `Error (Failed <the host's message>)` instead of
`Not_permitted` — still exactly once.

### Tasks (`Task.t`)

Composable async operations — a continuation monad. Tasks are pure descriptions; they do not execute until `run` is called. Use `let*` / `let+` syntax from `Task.Syntax` for readable chaining.

```ocaml
type 'a Task.t                                         (* async operation producing 'a *)

Task.return : 'a -> 'a Task.t                          (* wrap a pure value *)
Task.from_callback : (('a -> unit) -> unit) -> 'a Task.t  (* bridge callback-style async *)
Task.map  : ('a -> 'b) -> 'a Task.t -> 'b Task.t      (* transform result *)
Task.bind : ('a -> 'b Task.t) -> 'a Task.t -> 'b Task.t   (* sequence two tasks *)
Task.run  : 'a Task.t -> ('a -> unit) -> unit          (* execute and observe result *)

(* Guarded bridges for platform interop — a synchronous raise inside the body
   becomes Error (on_exn e) instead of leaving the task unresolved forever. *)
Task.guard : on_exn:(exn -> 'e) -> ((('a, 'e) result -> unit) -> unit)
  -> ('a, 'e) result Task.t
Task.guard_once : on_exn:(exn -> 'e) -> ((('a, 'e) result -> unit) -> unit)
  -> ('a, 'e) result Task.t

(* Prefer guard_once in any backend whose body can deliver an outcome
   SYNCHRONOUSLY. guard is `try f resolve with e -> resolve (Error (on_exn e))`,
   so its handler holds the resolver the task was run with. Delivering runs the
   application's dispatch, which is arbitrary code: if that raises, guard catches
   it and delivers a SECOND outcome, blaming the platform for an application bug.
   A latch written inside the body shadows only the body's own deliveries and
   cannot prevent this — guard_once latches the resolver before installing the
   handler, which is the only placement that covers both. A raise reaching the
   handler after an outcome was delivered is absorbed; a raise before any
   delivery still becomes Error (on_exn e). `just lint-classes` fails a latch
   written inside a Task.guard body. *)

(* Cancellation *)
type Task.cancellation_token
Task.cancellable : (Task.cancellation_token -> 'a Task.t)
  -> Task.cancellation_token * ('a, string) result Task.t
Task.cancel         : Task.cancellation_token -> unit       (* idempotent *)
Task.set_on_cancel  : Task.cancellation_token -> (unit -> unit) -> unit
Task.is_cancelled   : Task.cancellation_token -> bool

(* Syntax — open Task.Syntax for let operators *)
module Task.Syntax : sig
  val ( let* ) : 'a Task.t -> ('a -> 'b Task.t) -> 'b Task.t   (* bind *)
  val ( let+ ) : 'a Task.t -> ('a -> 'b) -> 'b Task.t          (* map *)
end
```

### Subscriptions (`Sub.t`)

Ongoing event sources managed by the runtime. All subscriptions are keyed for identity-based diffing.

```ocaml
Sub.none                                                        (* no subs *)
Sub.batch : 'msg Sub.t list -> 'msg Sub.t                       (* combine *)
Sub.every : string -> int -> (unit -> 'msg) -> 'msg Sub.t       (* timer, key + ms *)
Sub.on_keydown : string -> (string -> 'msg) -> 'msg Sub.t       (* global keydown *)
Sub.on_key : string -> key:string -> prevent:bool -> 'msg -> 'msg Sub.t   (* one folded key string *)
Sub.on_keyup : string -> (string -> 'msg) -> 'msg Sub.t         (* global keyup *)
Sub.on_resize : string -> (int -> int -> 'msg) -> 'msg Sub.t    (* window resize *)
Sub.on_visibility_change : string -> (bool -> 'msg) -> 'msg Sub.t
Sub.on_viewport_change : string -> (Nopal_element.Viewport.t -> 'msg) -> 'msg Sub.t  (* viewport changes *)
Sub.on_keydown_prevent : string -> (string -> ('msg * bool) option) -> 'msg Sub.t    (* keydown + preventDefault *)
Sub.custom : string -> (('msg -> unit) -> unit -> unit) -> 'msg Sub.t  (* setup returns cleanup *)
Sub.map : ('a -> 'b) -> 'a Sub.t -> 'b Sub.t
```

**Key strings are modifier-folded.** The string a keydown/keyup handler receives — and the string `on_key`'s `~key:` is compared against — folds the modifiers held during the event into the key name the platform reports. A held Ctrl becomes the prefix `Ctrl+`, a held Shift becomes `Shift+`, and when both are held they appear in the canonical order `Ctrl+Shift+key`, which is the only accepted spelling of a two-modifier chord. With neither held the key name passes through unchanged. Handlers match the whole string, never a substring: `"ArrowDown"` names bare ArrowDown and does not match Ctrl+ArrowDown, and `"Shift+Tab"` names Shift+Tab and does not match Ctrl+Shift+Tab.

Letter case is the platform's own and differs between the two modifiers: Ctrl leaves a letter lowercase while Shift uppercases it, and Ctrl does not suppress that uppercasing — the chord on the D key is `"Ctrl+d"` under Ctrl alone, `"Shift+D"` under Shift alone and `"Ctrl+Shift+D"` under both. Punctuation that needs Shift to type arrives with Shift held, so it carries the prefix and the bare mark matches nothing: the question mark is `"Shift+?"`, while the bare key on that same physical key is `"/"` on a US layout.

A keypress of the Ctrl or Shift key itself carries no prefixes at all, whichever other modifier is held, and reports the platform's own name: `"Control"` and `"Shift"`, which are not the prefix tokens `Ctrl+` and `Shift+`. A subscription matching a bare Ctrl press writes `~key:"Control"`; one matching a chord writes `~key:"Ctrl+d"`. Those two are the only key names exempt from prefixing — a keydown of the Alt key while Ctrl is held is `"Ctrl+Alt"`.

Only Ctrl and Shift are folded, so a subscription naming a bare key still matches an Alt chord and a Meta chord — neither flag is read. The fold applies to these window-level key subscriptions only: `Element.input ~on_keydown` receives the platform's raw key name with no prefixes on it.

### Element DSL (`nopal_element`)

`Element.t` is an exposed (not abstract) variant type so renderers can pattern-match exhaustively.

**Attribute precedence.** Where a builder takes both `?attrs` and a typed field
a backend renders as an attribute — `placeholder`, a radio's `name`, a picker's
`accept`/`capture`/`multiple`, `disabled`, a container's `focusable`, an
input's `required`/`autocomplete`/`input_type`/`name`, a form's
`autocomplete`/`novalidate`, a button's `button_type`/`disabled`, a link's
`destination` (its `href`, `rel` and `target`), a heading's `level` (its `role`,
`aria-level` and `data-nopal-heading`) — the rule is: **typed-field derivations beat the `~attrs` list; within the list, the
last pair wins.**

Those are two tiers, and they are not the same tier. A typed field sits *above*
the list, so `?attrs` is an escape hatch for keys the DSL does not model and
cannot overrule the ones it does. A pair a component puts *into* that list sits
*inside* it, so a caller's later pair of the same name replaces it.

The second tier is where a `nopal_ui` component's `role`, `aria-describedby`
and `data-field` travel. They are ordinary list pairs, so a caller passing the
same key through the component's own attributes replaces them — `Modal`,
`Navigation_bar`, `Bottom_tabs` and `Button` each document that as a deliberate
override rather than an accident, and it is the escape hatch a consumer reaches
for instead of abandoning the component.

A derivation that is *absent* leaves the caller's pair standing — a picker with
no `capture` does not erase a `capture` the caller declared, because the typed
field saying nothing is not the same as it saying "no attribute". A derivation
declines in one of two shapes:

- **Bool** — `true` asserts the key and `false` emits nothing, so a `false`
  uncovers a caller's pair and cannot remove it: `disabled`, `multiple`, an
  input's `required` (with the `aria-required` it carries), a form's
  `novalidate`, a button's `aria-disabled` (from its `disabled`).
- **Option or empty list** — absent asserts nothing and uncovers the caller's
  pair: `accept`, `capture`, an input's `autocomplete`, an input's `type` (from
  `input_type`), an input's `name`, a form's `autocomplete`.
- **By destination** — a link's `rel` is `"noopener noreferrer"` on an
  `External` or a `New_tab` link and absent on a `Route` link, and its `target`
  is `"_blank"` on a `New_tab` link and absent on the other two, so a caller's
  `rel` pair stands on a `Route` link only and a caller's `target` on a `Route`
  or an `External` link.

Some derivations have no absent form and are derived on every render, so a
caller's pair of that key is always replaced: `placeholder`, a radio's `name`,
a checkbox's, radio's or file picker's `type`, a button's `type` (from
`button_type`, which is `"button"` when the button names none), a link's
`href` (the `Route` or `New_tab` path, or the `External` URL), and a heading's `role`
(`"heading"`), `aria-level` (the level's digit, `"1"` to `"6"`) and
`data-nopal-heading` (`""`).

`nopal_web` and `nopal_test` are the two renderers that enforce this: the web
backend applies `?attrs` before it writes any derivation, and the structural
renderer appends derived pairs after the view's own and resolves every lookup —
`attr`, a `By_attr` selector, and the selector an event simulation
resolves — to the last pair. The first tier is shared by the two on the keys the
web backend writes as real attributes: `disabled`, `accept`, `capture`,
`multiple`, `placeholder`, a radio's `name`, a control's `type`, an input's
`required`, `aria-required`, `autocomplete` and `name`, a form's `autocomplete` and
`novalidate`, a button's `type` and `aria-disabled`, a link's `href` and
`rel`, a heading's `role`, `aria-level` and `data-nopal-heading`, a drawing's
`role`, `aria-label` and `aria-hidden`, and an image's
`alt`. Every one of them
carries the same value in both renderers except `disabled`, `multiple`,
`required` and `novalidate`, which are a presence attribute (`""`) in the DOM
and `"true"` in the structural tree — the two agree on which side wins, not on
the value. `aria-required` and a button's `aria-disabled` are `"true"` in both,
a button's `type` is `"button"` or `"submit"` in both, a link's `rel` is
`"noopener noreferrer"` in both, a heading's `role` is `"heading"`, its
`aria-level` the level's digit and its `data-nopal-heading` `""` in both, a
drawing's `role` is `"img"` and its
`aria-hidden` `"true"` in both, and a decorative image's `alt` is present and
`""` in both. A
checkbox's, radio's or file picker's `type` is the structural node's tag; an
input's `type` is a pair in both renderers. A container's
`focusable` is a first-tier derivation in both, but each spells it in its own
vocabulary — a tab-order attribute in the browser, `focusable` in the structural
tree — so there is no shared key to compare. `checked`, `value` and `selected`
are outside that — the browser carries all three as JS properties and
never as attributes, so a caller's pair of one of those names is not overruled
there. `nopal_test` still overlays them as derived pairs, so a structural
assertion on one of the three states what that renderer answers and is not
evidence about the browser. `Element.draw` and `Element.image` take no `attrs`
list, so the pairs each derives from its required `name` (see Graphic names,
below) are the only source of those keys and there is no caller pair for them
to outrank; should either gain an `attrs` list, its `name` outranks it under
this rule. No backend that has not been
written is bound by a test nobody has written.

**Submit contract.** An Enter in an `Element.input` can be answered by more
than one handler, and one sentence chooses: **the nearest handler that accepts
the Enter consumes it.** An Enter reaches at most one of the three handlers
below, and a handler the application supplied is never silently dropped. One
Enter can still dispatch two messages: an Enter deferred to the form is the
platform's implicit submission, which clicks the form's default button, so that
button's `on_click` comes first and the form's `on_submit` second (see below).
Three handlers, nearest first:

1. **The input's `on_keydown`** is consulted for every key. Its `'msg option`
   return is the consumption signal: `Some msg` dispatches `msg` and consumes
   the key; `None` declines it.
2. **The input's `on_submit`** answers an Enter that `on_keydown` declined, or
   any Enter on an input with no `on_keydown`. It answers Enter and no other
   key. Supplying both handlers is meaningful: `on_keydown` answers the keys it
   cares about and returns `None` for the rest, and an Enter it declines still
   submits.
3. **The nearest enclosing `Element.form`'s `on_submit`** answers an Enter
   neither of the input's handlers answered. An input with no enclosing form, or
   in a form that authors no `on_submit`, dispatches nothing for it.

**Only Enter suppresses the platform default.** An Enter answered by either of
the input's own handlers prevents the default, so the enclosing form does not
also submit. A consuming `on_keydown` on any other key leaves that key's default
alone, so a handler that records every keystroke does not stop its own input
receiving text.

**The cost of mixing levels.** An input carrying its own `on_submit` answers the
Enter itself, so the enclosing form never sees it: in a form where one field has
`on_submit`, Enter in that field dispatches a different message than Enter
anywhere else in the form. Author submission at one level — the form, or each
input — and do not mix the two.

Both renderers take the route from `Submit_route.of_key`, one pure definition,
so the web renderer and the structural test renderer answer every keydown alike.
What a deferred Enter and a button press then do is the platform's share, and
both renderers answer it alike too: the web renderer leaves it to the browser,
and `Test_renderer.click` and `Test_renderer.keydown` model it.

- **A button submits only when it says so.** `Element.button
  ~button_type:Submit` is a submit button: clicking it inside a `Form`
  dispatches its own `on_click` and then the form's `on_submit`. A button that
  names no type is `Push`, renders `type="button"`, and dispatches its
  `on_click` alone, inside a form or not, so a "show password" toggle or a
  cancel needs nothing extra. A `("type", _)` pair in `~attrs` never takes
  effect on a button.
- **An unanswered Enter in a field clicks the form's default button**, the
  first submit button in tree order. Enabled, it dispatches its `on_click` and
  then the form's `on_submit`. Disabled, the Enter dispatches nothing, even
  when an enabled submit button follows it.
- **With no submit button, a form submits on Enter only when it holds a single
  field that blocks implicit submission.** Every `Element.input` counts,
  whatever its `input_type`; a checkbox, radio, select or file picker does not.
  A form with two inputs and no submit button dispatches nothing on Enter, in
  either renderer. An input whose type a caller overrides through `~attrs` to a
  kind the browser does not count (`hidden`, say) is outside the structural
  model.
- **A disabled button is inert and stays focusable.** `~disabled:true` renders
  `aria-disabled="true"`, not the native `disabled` attribute: the button stays
  in the tab order, is announced as disabled, and cancels its own activation,
  so neither a click nor an Enter it would answer dispatches or submits
  anything. A focused button that becomes disabled keeps focus. A caller who
  wants the native attribute can still spell it through `~attrs`, but that
  route is outside the structural model: the browser treats such a button as
  disabled, while the structural renderer answers it as enabled. `disabled`
  changes no styling; pass a `~style` for the disabled look.

A `Form` that authors no `on_submit` still cancels the platform's submission:
its only submit listener calls `preventDefault`, so wrapping fields for the
landmark or `autocomplete` alone never turns Enter or a button press into a page
reload. Do not nest one form inside another — nested forms are invalid HTML
whose recovery each browser decides for itself; nothing rejects one, and
"nearest enclosing form" assumes there is at most one. A form becomes a landmark
for assistive technology only once it has an accessible name, which travels
through `~attrs` (an `("aria-label", …)` pair, for instance).

**Link children.** Give a link no interactive children (Button, Checkbox,
Input): the child dispatches its own message and then the link's. An ancestor's
`on_click` also fires, since the click propagates. The web anchor is
`display: inline`, so under Button or Scroll its width, height and vertical
padding have no effect; wrap it in a Box to size it.

**Links.** `Element.link` is a real link wherever the platform has one: a
native `<a>` in a browser or webview, so the link role, the URL on hover,
middle- and modified-click, "Open in new tab" and "Copy link address" all come
from the platform. A link never takes a raw `href`. Its destination is one of:

- `Link.Route { path; on_follow }` — in-app. `path` is a `Route_path.t` and
  `on_follow` is required: a followed link dispatches it, and the
  application's `update` answers with `Router.push`. Build both from one route
  with `Router.destination` (see Routing) so the address and the navigation
  cannot drift apart. The link itself never touches history.
- `Link.External { url; on_open_failed }` — outside the app. `url` is a
  `Url.t`, and `on_open_failed` is required: it is dispatched with a typed
  `Link.open_error` when a host's opener cannot show the URL. A browser follows
  an external link itself and never dispatches it. An external anchor carries
  `rel="noopener noreferrer"`, so the opened page cannot reach back.
- `Link.New_tab { path }` — a path on the page's own origin (a photo, a file,
  a page the server serves beside the app), opened in a new tab. `path` is a
  `Route_path.t`, so it starts with a single `/`. The anchor carries
  `target="_blank"` and `rel="noopener noreferrer"`, and `decide` leaves every
  click on it to the platform on either host, so it dispatches nothing. Reach
  for it where a `Route` link would be taken over and navigate in place, and
  an `External` link cannot carry the path because it has no scheme.

All three are checked at construction and neither has an unchecked constructor, so
`javascript:`, `data:` and protocol-relative paths are unconstructible:

- `Url.of_string` accepts a scheme of `http`, `https`, `mailto` or `tel`
  (any case) followed by `:`, and examines nothing after it. It refuses
  `Missing_scheme` (no scheme, or none a browser reads as one),
  `Unsupported_scheme` (with the scheme as written) and `Control_character`.
- `Route_path.of_string` accepts a string starting with exactly one `/` not
  followed by `/` or `\` — `"/"` and `"/a/b?q=1#h"` pass. It refuses
  `Not_absolute` (no leading `/`, which covers `"javascript:…"` and `""`),
  `Protocol_relative` (`"//host"`, `"/\host"`, both of which a browser resolves
  to another host) and `Control_character`.
- Both refuse a control character (U+0000–U+001F, U+007F) anywhere and a space
  at either end, checked first, because browsers strip those before reading a
  URL. Every error case carries the refused `input`, and `to_string` returns
  the accepted input unchanged.

What a click does is `Link.decide ~host click destination`, one pure, native
function every renderer calls, so the browser, the webview and the structural
renderer cannot answer differently:

| Host | Click | `Route` | `External` | `New_tab` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Browser` | `Primary`, no modifier | `Navigate on_follow` | `Leave_to_platform` | `Leave_to_platform` |
| `Browser` | `Primary` with Ctrl, Meta, Shift or Alt; `Middle`; `Other` | `Leave_to_platform` | `Leave_to_platform` | `Leave_to_platform` |
| `Webview` | `Primary` or `Middle`, any modifiers | `Navigate on_follow` | `Open_externally url` | `Leave_to_platform` |
| `Webview` | `Other` | `Leave_to_platform` | `Leave_to_platform` | `Leave_to_platform` |

`Navigate` prevents the platform default and dispatches the message once;
`Leave_to_platform` neither prevents nor dispatches, so the browser opens a
tab, window or page as it decides; `Open_externally` prevents the default and
hands the URL to the host's opener, dispatching `on_open_failed` when that
fails. A webview has no tabs, so a modified or middle click on a `Route` link
is a plain click there, a click on a `New_tab` link is the webview's to handle
(nopal does not test what it does with `target="_blank"`), and a click on an external link never navigates the webview off
the app (the context menu's "Open Link" and a dragged link are not guarded). Keyboard Enter on a focused link reaches `decide` as an unmodified
primary click, and a link is in the tab order natively. Which host a link is
rendered for is the mount's choice: `Nopal_web.mount` renders for `Browser`,
and for `Webview` when given `~open_external` (Tauri apps: `Nopal_tauri_mount`).

**Headings.** `Element.heading level child` is a heading wherever the platform
has one: a native `<h1>`–`<h6>` of its level in a browser or webview, so it is
in the document outline and in assistive technology's heading navigation. The
level is the closed `heading_level`, `H1` to `H6`, so a level 0 or 7 cannot be
built. A heading takes one child, as `button` and `link` do; a heading made of
several runs takes a `row` as its child. A heading is not a flex container.

The level is semantics, not appearance. Nopal ships no type scale. How a
heading looks — its size, weight, colour and spacing — comes from its own
`style`, applied to the heading itself with no wrapper, and two headings of
different levels with the same `style` look the same. The level is typed, so a
`role` or `aria-level` pair in `~attrs` never takes effect (see Attribute
precedence above): a heading is always announced as a heading of its level.

On the web the browser's own heading margin, font size and weight are
neutralised, so an unstyled heading looks like the text around it. **This is the
only user-agent default Nopal neutralises.** An unstyled `button` still shows
the browser's padding, border and background, and an unstyled `link` its
colour and underline. The heading does not follow them because `Style.layout`
has no margin, so a leaked heading margin could not be removed by any style.
The reset is one rule at the top of every mount's `<style data-nopal>` sheet:

```css
:where([data-nopal-heading]){margin:0;font-size:inherit;font-weight:inherit}
```

It selects only the `data-nopal-heading` marker Nopal writes on its own
headings, so a heading on the host page around the mount point keeps the
browser's defaults. The whole selector sits inside `:where`, which gives it zero
specificity: it beats the user agent and nothing else, and a heading's own
style wins whether it is written inline or, when it has interaction states, as
a class rule. A second mount carries a second, identical copy.

**Heading order is guidance, not enforcement.** Order the headings of a view as
an outline: one `H1` for the view, and no level skipped on the way down, so an
`H2` is followed by an `H3` and not an `H4`. Going back up may skip, as an `H4`
closing a section followed by the next `H2` does. Nopal does not check this,
and nothing rejects a view that breaks it: the type cannot express it, and a
run-time check could only log the breach. Check it in a browser with axe's
`heading-order` rule. That is a best-practice rule, not a WCAG one, so an axe
run restricted to the WCAG tags, as `test/e2e/tests/axe.ts` is, does not run
it. Name it by rule id instead, as `test/e2e/tests/kitchen-sink-headings.spec.ts`
does with `withRules(["heading-order", "empty-heading", "aria-allowed-role"])`.

```ocaml
Element.empty                                                    (* renders nothing *)
Element.text : string -> 'msg Element.t                          (* plain text *)
Element.styled_text : text_style:Text.t -> string -> 'msg Element.t

(* Layout containers — Box supports pointer + wheel events for pan/zoom, and focus
   edges covering its whole subtree *)
type pointer_event = { x : float; y : float; client_x : float; client_y : float }
type wheel_event = { delta_y : float; x : float; y : float }

Element.box    : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?focusable:bool -> ?on_focus:'msg -> ?on_blur:'msg
  -> ?on_pointer_move:(pointer_event -> 'msg) -> ?on_pointer_leave:'msg
  -> ?on_pointer_down:(pointer_event -> 'msg) -> ?on_pointer_up:(pointer_event -> 'msg)
  -> ?on_wheel:(wheel_event -> 'msg) -> 'msg Element.t list -> 'msg Element.t
  (* [focusable] places the container in the platform's own keyboard traversal
     order, so an application never spells a raw tab-order attribute for it; each
     backend decides how a focusable container is reached. It defaults to off, and
     a container that is not focusable still reports focus arriving on a focusable
     descendant.
     [on_focus] and [on_blur] are scoped to the whole subtree, not to the container
     alone. Focus arriving from outside the container — on the container itself or
     on anything inside it — is an arrival, and only focus leaving the container
     and everything inside it is a departure. A move between two elements that are
     both inside the container dispatches nothing, so a panel revealed on
     [on_focus] survives the user reaching a control inside that panel. Nested
     containers therefore overlap: focus landing inside the inner one is an
     arrival for it and for every enclosing container too, each dispatching its
     own message. *)
Element.row    : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list -> 'msg Element.t list -> 'msg Element.t
Element.column : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list -> 'msg Element.t list -> 'msg Element.t

(* Forms — a submission group. See "Submit contract" above for how an Enter in
   a field reaches the form. *)
type autocomplete_mode = On | Off
Element.autocomplete_mode_to_string : autocomplete_mode -> string   (* "on" | "off" — sole producer *)
Element.form : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?on_submit:'msg -> ?autocomplete:autocomplete_mode -> ?novalidate:bool
  -> 'msg Element.t list -> 'msg Element.t
  (* A container like Element.box, laying its children down the page unless
     [style] asks for the other direction. [on_submit] is dispatched once per
     submission — an Enter a field deferred to the form, or a button typed
     Submit pressed — and a submission never navigates, whether or not
     [on_submit] is authored. A button that names no type does not submit, and
     a disabled one submits by no route. [autocomplete] asks the platform to offer, or not, remembered
     values for every field; absent, it asks for nothing. [novalidate] (default
     false) skips the platform's own constraint validation. On a backend with no
     native form the group is an ordinary container and the Enter routing still
     holds. *)

(* Interactive elements *)
type button_type = Submit | Push
Element.button_type_to_string : button_type -> string   (* "submit" | "button" — sole producer *)
Element.button : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?button_type:button_type -> ?disabled:bool
  -> ?on_click:'msg -> ?on_dblclick:'msg -> 'msg Element.t -> 'msg Element.t
  (* [button_type] (default Push) says whether activating the button submits the
     enclosing Form: Submit dispatches on_click and then the form's on_submit;
     Push dispatches on_click alone. [disabled] (default false) keeps the button
     focusable and makes it inert: a click, or an Enter in a field for which it
     is the form's default button, dispatches nothing and submits nothing.
     It renders aria-disabled="true", not the native disabled attribute that
     Element.checkbox, radio and select use, so the button stays in the tab
     order. Both are typed: a ("type", _) pair in [attrs] never takes effect,
     and an ("aria-disabled", _) pair only while [disabled] is false. *)
type input_type = Plain | Password | Email | Tel | Url | Number | Search
Element.input_type_to_string : input_type -> string
  (* "text" | "password" | "email" | "tel" | "url" | "number" | "search" — sole producer *)
Element.input : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?placeholder:string -> ?on_change:(string -> 'msg) -> ?on_submit:'msg
  -> ?on_focus:'msg -> ?on_blur:'msg -> ?on_keydown:(string -> 'msg option)
  -> ?required:bool -> ?autocomplete:string -> ?input_type:input_type
  -> ?name:string -> string -> 'msg Element.t
  (* [on_focus] fires when the input takes focus and [on_blur] when it loses it.
     An input holds no children, so neither edge has a subtree to account for —
     unlike the same-named arguments on Element.box.
     [required] (default false) marks the field as one a submission needs, to
     the platform's constraint validation and to assistive technology
     (aria-required). Its invalid appearance is the browser's own and is not
     stylable: Interaction has no invalid state. [autocomplete] is the per-field
     token — "username", "current-password", "email", … — passed through as
     written. [input_type] is closed on purpose: a checkbox, radio or file
     picker has its own element; any other kind stays reachable through a
     ("type", …) pair in [attrs], which an input authoring no [input_type]
     leaves standing. [name] is the key the field's value is submitted under,
     and the one a password manager reads to recognise it. Each of the four
     outranks an [attrs] pair of its key, so adopting one makes that pair stop
     taking effect; an input authoring none of them leaves the pair standing. *)
Element.checkbox : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?disabled:bool -> ?on_toggle:(bool -> 'msg) -> bool -> 'msg Element.t
Element.radio : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?checked:bool -> ?disabled:bool -> ?on_select:'msg -> name:string -> unit -> 'msg Element.t
type select_option = { value : string; label : string; disabled : bool }
Element.select_option : ?disabled:bool -> value:string -> string -> select_option
Element.select : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?disabled:bool -> ?on_change:(string -> 'msg) -> selected:string
  -> select_option list -> 'msg Element.t

(* Links — see "Links" above for the destination, the checks and the decide
   table. *)
Element.link : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> 'msg Link.destination -> 'msg Element.t -> 'msg Element.t
  (* Renders an anchor (tag "a" in both renderers) whose href is the Route or
     New_tab path or the External URL, with rel="noopener noreferrer" on
     External and New_tab, and target="_blank" on New_tab only. All three keys
     are typed: an ("href", _) pair in [attrs] never takes effect, a ("rel", _)
     pair only on a Route link, and a ("target", _) pair only on a Route or an
     External link. *)

(* Headings — see "Headings" above for the reset and the order guidance. *)
type heading_level = H1 | H2 | H3 | H4 | H5 | H6
Element.heading_level_to_int : heading_level -> int   (* 1 … 6 — sole producer of the tag digit and aria-level *)
Element.equal_heading_level : heading_level -> heading_level -> bool
Element.heading : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> heading_level -> 'msg Element.t -> 'msg Element.t
  (* Renders tag "h1" … "h6" in both renderers, with role="heading",
     aria-level="<1-6>" and data-nopal-heading="" written after [attrs], so a
     ("role", _), ("aria-level", _) or ("data-nopal-heading", _) pair in
     [attrs] never takes effect. The level is semantics only: the look is
     [style]. A level change on update replaces the web node with a new <hN>.
     Arm: Heading of { style; interaction; attrs; level : heading_level;
     child : 'msg t }, after Link. *)

module Url : sig                       (* Nopal_element.Url — pure, native *)
  type t                               (* abstract: only of_string makes one *)
  type error =
    | Missing_scheme of { input : string }
    | Unsupported_scheme of { input : string; scheme : string }  (* scheme as written *)
    | Control_character of { input : string }   (* also a space at either end *)
  val of_string : string -> (t, error) result   (* http | https | mailto | tel, any case *)
  val to_string : t -> string                   (* the accepted input, unchanged *)
end

module Route_path : sig                (* Nopal_element.Route_path — pure, native *)
  type t                               (* abstract: only of_string makes one *)
  type error =
    | Not_absolute of { input : string }        (* no leading "/", incl. "javascript:…" and "" *)
    | Protocol_relative of { input : string }   (* second character "/" or "\" *)
    | Control_character of { input : string }   (* also a space at either end *)
  val of_string : string -> (t, error) result
  val to_string : t -> string                   (* the accepted input, unchanged *)
end

module Link : sig                      (* Nopal_element.Link — pure, native *)
  type open_error =
    | Not_permitted       (* the host refused: no permission, or none for this URL *)
    | Failed of string    (* the opener failed; a human-readable reason that never carries the URL *)
  type 'msg destination =
    | Route of { path : Route_path.t; on_follow : 'msg }
    | External of { url : Url.t; on_open_failed : open_error -> 'msg }
    | New_tab of { path : Route_path.t }   (* same origin, new tab; never taken over *)
  type button = Primary | Middle | Other
  type click = { button : button; ctrl : bool; meta : bool; shift : bool; alt : bool }
  type host = Browser | Webview
  type 'msg action =
    | Navigate of 'msg            (* prevent the default, dispatch once *)
    | Leave_to_platform           (* no prevent, no dispatch *)
    | Open_externally of Url.t    (* prevent the default, hand the URL to the opener *)
  val decide : host:host -> click -> 'msg destination -> 'msg action   (* total *)
  val map_destination : ('a -> 'b) -> 'a destination -> 'b destination
end

(* File selection. Bytes never cross into OCaml: [blob_id] is an opaque handle
   only a _web backend can resolve, via Nopal_blob_web.Blob_store.lookup. *)
type capture = User | Environment
Element.capture_to_string : capture -> string   (* "user" | "environment" — sole producer *)
type file_info = {
  blob_id : string;       (* opaque store handle; never fabricate one *)
  name : string;
  size : int;             (* byte length *)
  mime : string;          (* user-agent report — a hint, never validation *)
  last_modified : float;  (* ms since the POSIX epoch *)
}
Element.file_info : blob_id:string -> name:string -> size:int -> mime:string
  -> last_modified:float -> file_info
Element.file_input : ?style:Style.t -> ?interaction:Interaction.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?accept:string list -> ?capture:capture -> ?multiple:bool
  -> ?on_change:(file_info list -> 'msg) -> unit -> 'msg Element.t
  (* [accept] is a picker hint, never a gate. Clearing the picker fires
     [on_change] with [[]] rather than nothing. Blob lifetime is the
     application's: handles live for the page session until released. *)

(* Media and scrolling *)
Element.image  : ?style:Style.t -> ?fit:Element.image_fit -> src:string
  -> name:Graphic_name.t -> unit -> 'msg Element.t
  (* [name] is the only source of the text alternative: [Named n] writes
     alt="n"; [Decorative] writes alt="" (present and empty, which removes the
     image from the accessibility tree — an absent alt would not). An SVG shown
     through an image is named here: assistive technology ignores the SVG
     document's own attributes.
     [fit] says how the picture is drawn into the box [style] sizes; the web
     backend writes it as object-fit. Absent, the platform default stands, which
     on the web stretches the picture to the box. It is the image's own field,
     not a style one, because it means nothing on any other element. *)
type Element.image_fit =
  | Contain   (* the whole picture, as large as the box allows *)
  | Cover     (* the box filled; what falls outside it is cut off *)
val Element.image_fit_to_string : image_fit -> string   (* "contain" | "cover" *)
val Element.equal_image_fit : image_fit -> image_fit -> bool
Element.scroll : ?style:Style.t -> ?attrs:(string * string) list
  -> ?reveal:Reveal.t -> 'msg Element.t -> 'msg Element.t
  (* [reveal] names a keyed descendant that must be brought into view, and the
     alignment it should come to rest under. It is a request, not an invariant:
     a backend acts on it when it changes and at no other time, so a reader who
     scrolls away from the named child keeps their position. Omitting it asks
     for nothing, and a container that asks for nothing behaves exactly as it
     did before the argument existed.

     [attrs] are application attributes carried to the rendered container as
     written — the container's own identity, so a platform request can name it
     directly instead of reaching it through a wrapper. An [id] here is the
     spelling Cmd.scroll_by resolves against. Names and values are opaque
     application strings, never interpreted, and the list is compared in order,
     so two containers carrying the same pairs in a different order are not
     equal. Do not put [style] or [class] in it: both belong to the renderer,
     and a [style] pair here overwrites the whole inline style the renderer
     wrote on the container — the overflow that makes it scroll included — so
     the container silently stops scrolling. *)

(* Identity for list reconciliation, and for naming a scroll container's
   reveal target *)
Element.keyed : string -> 'msg Element.t -> 'msg Element.t
  (* Keys must be unique within the container that holds them; where a key is
     repeated, the first match in document order is the one that resolves. Keys
     are opaque application strings and are compared and resolved as written,
     so any punctuation is safe to use. *)

(* Bringing a child of a scroll container into view — pure, native-compiling,
   references nothing else in the package *)
module Reveal : sig
  type align = Nearest | Start | Center | End_   (* [End_]: [end] is a keyword *)
  type t = { key : string; align : align }
  val nearest : string -> t
  val start : string -> t
  val center : string -> t
  val end_ : string -> t
  val align_token : align -> string  (* "nearest" | "start" | "center" | "end";
                                        the sole producer of the string form *)
  val equal : t -> t -> bool
  val should_reveal : previous:t option -> next:t option -> bool
  val offset_for :
    scroll_offset:float -> viewport_height:float -> content_height:float ->
    child_top:float -> child_height:float -> align:align -> float option
end
  (* [should_reveal] is the whole rule: act when a container that carried no
     request gains one, and when a request changes in either its key or its
     alignment; do nothing when it is unchanged, withdrawn, or never existed.
     The effect is therefore edge-triggered — resizing the visible area with an
     unchanged request re-asserts nothing, and the requested child can sit
     outside the visible area until the request next changes.

     That decision is portable and so is [offset_for]; taking the measurements
     and moving the container are each backend's own concern, and on a backend
     that does not render elements the request is inert, which is not an error.

     [offset_for]'s six measurements share one origin, the top of the
     container's scrollable content, so [child_top] does not change as the
     container scrolls. It is total: the result is clamped to an offset the
     container can take, and [None] means either that the alignment asks for
     the offset the container already holds or that a measurement is not
     finite. A child taller than [viewport_height] falls back to showing its
     top edge under every alignment. *)

(* Which handler answers a keydown on an input — the submit contract as one
   pure, native-compiling definition both renderers call; references nothing
   else in the package *)
module Submit_route : sig
  type 'msg t =
    | Dispatch of { msg : 'msg; prevent_default : bool }
        (* a handler on the input answered; prevent_default is true exactly
           when the key is Enter *)
    | To_enclosing_form   (* an Enter nothing on the input answered *)
    | Nothing             (* any other key nothing answered; never reaches a form *)
  val of_key :
    key:string -> on_keydown:(string -> 'msg option) option ->
    on_submit:'msg option -> 'msg t   (* total *)
end

(* Moving a scroll container by an amount relative to its own visible height —
   pure, native-compiling, references nothing else in the package. The command
   that carries one of these is Cmd.scroll_by. *)
module Scroll_delta : sig
  type t   (* abstract; ordering operators deliberately withheld *)
  val viewports : float -> t
  val equal : t -> t -> bool
  val offset_for :
    scroll_offset:float -> viewport_height:float -> content_height:float ->
    t -> float option
end
  (* [viewports n] is a movement of [n] times the container's visible height,
     positive toward the end and negative back toward the start. It accepts any
     float, including a non-finite one: the rejection lives at [offset_for],
     which answers [None], so nothing validates on the way in. The type is
     abstract so a later pixel or line unit can arrive without changing the
     command that carries it, and it withholds comparison operators because
     exact float comparison on a geometry quantity is a latent bug.

     [equal] is over [Float.equal] and answers "is this the same request",
     never "did the container move far enough". Exact in the tolerance sense —
     no epsilon — but not discriminating: [Float.equal] is [compare x y = 0], so
     [-0.0] equals [0.0] and a NaN equals a NaN, and nothing depends on either
     distinction. It exists for structural tests,
     which have no other way to read a value out of the abstract type; nothing
     that applies a request uses it.

     [offset_for]'s three measurements share one origin, the top of the
     container's scrollable content. The result is clamped to [0.] through
     [Float.max 0. (content_height -. viewport_height)], so it is always an
     offset the container can take. It is total, and [None] has exactly two
     causes: the clamped offset is the one the container already holds, or one
     of the measurements — or the delta — is not finite, in which case no
     offset is guessed. The first cause compares the clamped offset against the
     offset the container currently holds, never the delta against zero, so a
     container holding an offset outside its reachable range is pulled back into
     it — [Some] even for a delta of zero, and even where the container cannot
     scroll. A container that cannot scroll and already holds a reachable offset
     answers [None] to every delta, and so does a container at the end asked to
     move further. The arithmetic is portable; taking the measurements is each
     backend's own concern. *)

(* 2D canvas drawing *)
Element.draw : ?on_pointer_move:(pointer_event -> 'msg) -> ?on_click:(pointer_event -> 'msg)
  -> ?on_pointer_leave:'msg -> ?on_pointer_down:(pointer_event -> 'msg)
  -> ?on_pointer_up:(pointer_event -> 'msg) -> ?on_wheel:(wheel_event -> 'msg)
  -> ?cursor:Cursor.t -> name:Graphic_name.t
  -> width:float -> height:float -> Scene.t list -> 'msg Element.t
  (* [name] is the only source of the canvas's accessible attributes:
     [Named n] writes role="img" and aria-label="n"; [Decorative] writes
     aria-hidden="true" and neither of the other two. No other accessibility
     attribute is derived. *)

(* Graphic names — Nopal_element.Graphic_name, an alias of
   Nopal_scene.Graphic_name. Required by draw, image, Nopal_svg.render and
   every chart view; there is no default, so an author states which case a
   graphic is at the call site. *)
module Graphic_name : sig
  type t = private
    | Named of string   (* exposed as one image carrying this name *)
    | Decorative        (* absent from the accessibility tree *)
  type error = Blank of { input : string }
    (* empty, or every byte is ASCII whitespace (HT, LF, FF, CR, SP), a C0
       control (U+0000-U+001F) or DEL; NBSP and other Unicode spaces count
       as content *)
  val named : string -> (t, error) result   (* Ok keeps the input untrimmed *)
  val decorative : t
  val equal : t -> t -> bool
  val aria_attrs : t -> (string * string option) list
    (* the one name-to-attribute table every renderer answers from; a None
       value is a key to remove: Named n -> role=img, aria-label=n, no
       aria-hidden; Decorative -> aria-hidden=true, no role, no aria-label *)
  val image_alt : t -> string   (* the label, or "" for Decorative *)
end
(* [private]: match Named/Decorative exhaustively, build Named only through
   [named]. Decorative is a value of its own, never an empty name, so do not
   turn a refused name into [decorative]: that is the silence the type exists
   to prevent. The examples surface the refusal instead:

   let named_graphic label graphic =
     match Graphic_name.named label with
     | Ok name -> graphic name
     | Error (Graphic_name.Blank { input }) ->
         Element.text (Printf.sprintf "Refused a blank graphic name: %S" input)

   named_graphic "Monthly revenue, January to June" (fun name ->
     Element.draw ~name ~width:400.0 ~height:250.0 scene) *)

(* Virtualized list — renders only visible items for large datasets *)
module Virtual_list : sig
  module Positive_float : sig
    type t
    val of_float : float -> t option   (* None if <= 0 *)
    val to_float : t -> float
  end
  module Natural : sig
    type t
    val of_int : int -> t option       (* None if < 0 *)
    val to_int : t -> int
  end
  type fixed
  type 'height scroll_state
  val scroll_state : offset:float -> fixed scroll_state  (* clamps negative to 0 *)
  val offset : _ scroll_state -> float
  type range = { first : int; last : int }
  val visible_range :
    scroll_state:fixed scroll_state -> row_height:Positive_float.t ->
    container_height:Positive_float.t -> item_count:Natural.t ->
    overscan:Natural.t -> range
end

Element.virtual_list :
  ?style:Style.t -> ?on_scroll:(float -> 'msg) ->
  item_count:Virtual_list.Natural.t -> row_height:Virtual_list.Positive_float.t ->
  container_height:Virtual_list.Positive_float.t ->
  scroll_state:Virtual_list.fixed Virtual_list.scroll_state ->
  overscan:Virtual_list.Natural.t ->
  (int -> 'msg Element.t) -> 'msg Element.t

(* Message transform for component embedding *)
Element.map : ('a -> 'b) -> 'a Element.t -> 'b Element.t

(* Responsive combinators — select subtree or style by viewport size class *)
Element.responsive : Viewport.t -> compact:'msg Element.t -> ?medium:'msg Element.t
  -> expanded:'msg Element.t -> unit -> 'msg Element.t
Element.responsive_style : Viewport.t -> compact:Style.t -> ?medium:Style.t
  -> expanded:Style.t -> unit -> Style.t

(* Structural equality — functions compared by physical identity *)
Element.equal : 'msg Element.t -> 'msg Element.t -> bool
```

### Viewport (`nopal_element`)

Describes the current display surface — dimensions, size class, orientation, safe area insets.

```ocaml
type orientation = Portrait | Landscape
Viewport.make : width:int -> height:int -> ?safe_area:safe_area -> unit -> Viewport.t
Viewport.width : Viewport.t -> int
Viewport.height : Viewport.t -> int
Viewport.size_class : Viewport.t -> Size_class.t  (* Compact | Medium | Expanded *)
Viewport.orientation : Viewport.t -> orientation
Viewport.is_compact : Viewport.t -> bool
Viewport.is_medium : Viewport.t -> bool
Viewport.is_expanded : Viewport.t -> bool

(* Safe area insets *)
type safe_area
Viewport.make_safe_area : top:int -> right:int -> bottom:int -> left:int -> unit -> safe_area
Viewport.zero_insets : safe_area
Viewport.safe_area : Viewport.t -> safe_area
Viewport.safe_area_top : safe_area -> int
Viewport.safe_area_right : safe_area -> int
Viewport.safe_area_bottom : safe_area -> int
Viewport.safe_area_left : safe_area -> int

(* Equality *)

Viewport.equal : Viewport.t -> Viewport.t -> bool

(* Test presets *)
Viewport.phone : Viewport.t            (* 375×812, Compact, Portrait *)
Viewport.phone_landscape : Viewport.t  (* 812×375, Medium, Landscape *)
Viewport.tablet : Viewport.t           (* 768×1024, Medium, Portrait *)
Viewport.desktop : Viewport.t          (* 1440×900, Expanded, Landscape *)
```

### Style System (`nopal_style`)

All styling is typed — no CSS strings in view code.

```ocaml
(* Layout — all fields are optional; None means "no opinion" *)
type direction = Row_dir | Column_dir
type align = Start | Center | End_ | Space_between
(* The main axis (layout.main_align): justify-content flex-start, center,
   flex-end, space-between. No Stretch: the platform lays a main-axis stretch out
   exactly as Start, so a child fills this axis through flex_grow or Fill. *)
type cross_align = Start | Center | End_ | Stretch
(* The cross axis (layout.cross_align): align-items flex-start, center,
   flex-end, stretch. No Space_between: the platform drops it there and
   stretches. The constructor names are shared. In a layout field a bare
   constructor resolves to the field's type; an unannotated binding resolves to
   cross_align, the type defined last, so a value bound for main_align is
   annotated Style.align. *)
type size = Fill | Hug | Fixed of float | Fraction of float
(* Fixed is honoured on the axis the parent lays its children out along: the
   element is not squeezed below that size, whatever a sibling's content would
   prefer, and an element with no content of its own does not collapse away. The
   guarantee runs in the shrink direction only — a flex_grow set beside a Fixed
   size still makes the element larger, which is the caller asking for it. The
   other three stay flexible and may be given less room than they ask for — Fill
   takes what is left, which is how two Fill siblings in a row resolve to half
   each, and Fraction is reduced under pressure rather than held at its
   percentage. The guarantee covers the main axis only, which is the only axis
   where siblings compete for room, and only children of a container that lays
   its children out. The web backend gets it by emitting flex-shrink: 0 beside a
   Fixed main-axis size: width under a row parent, height under a column parent,
   and nothing for any other size, for the cross axis, or for a child of an
   element that is not a layout container. Three routes never get an axis at all
   and so never get the guard: a size declared in an interaction (hover, focused
   or pressed) style, a Draw element, which carries no Style.t, and a root
   mounted into a container the framework did not build. CONTRIBUTING.md's D-9
   records them. The axis is the parent's, not the element's own
   layout.direction — that field is emitted as this element's
   flex-direction and governs its children. *)

type layout = {
  direction : direction option; main_align : align option;
  cross_align : cross_align option; wrap : bool option; gap : float option;
  padding_top : float option; padding_right : float option;
  padding_bottom : float option; padding_left : float option;
  width : size option; height : size option; flex_grow : float option;
  min_width : float option; min_height : float option;
}
(* Style.default_layout has all fields None. *)
(* min_width and min_height are floors in pixels on the rendered box, and a
   floor of zero is not the same as no floor. A box this framework lays out is
   an item of its container's layout, and the platform gives such an item an
   automatic minimum equal to its own content — which is why an ancestor of a
   scrolling child grows to fit that child instead of letting it scroll, pushing
   whatever follows it out of view. Setting the floor to 0. hands the overflow
   back to the scrolling descendant; a larger floor is an ordinary minimum size;
   None leaves the platform default in place. A floor at or below a Fixed size
   on the axis the parent lays its children out along is inert, since such a
   size is already not squeezed below what it declares; a floor above it is not
   — CSS clamps the used size into the floor, so the box is used at the larger
   of the two, which is growth in the same direction flex_grow beside a Fixed
   size already allows. A floor does its work on a flexible size: Fill, Hug, or
   one carrying flex_grow. Unlike the shrink guard above, a floor needs no
   parent axis, because it states something about this element alone rather
   than about how it competes with a sibling for room; it
   is therefore emitted in an interaction (hover, focused or pressed) style too,
   and beside a Fixed size both declarations are emitted, neither displacing the
   other. The web backend emits min-width and min-height including the zero:
   min-height: 0px, never a dropped declaration. *)

(* Colors — defined in Color, a leaf module of nopal_style. Integer RGBA for CSS
   authoring; distinct from Nopal_scene.Color, the float 0.0-1.0 graphics type. *)
type Color.t = Rgba of { r : int; g : int; b : int; a : float }
             | Hex of string | Named of string | Transparent

Color.rgba        : int -> int -> int -> float -> Color.t
Color.hex         : string -> Color.t     (* taken as given; not validated *)
Color.named       : string -> Color.t     (* taken as given; not validated *)
Color.transparent : Color.t
Color.equal       : Color.t -> Color.t -> bool   (* Float.equal on alpha *)

(* Style.color is a manifest type equation onto Color.t, so both spellings
   construct and pattern-match the same four arms. The Style spelling is
   permanent and supported, not a deprecation shim. *)
type color = Color.t = Rgba of { r : int; g : int; b : int; a : float }
                     | Hex of string | Named of string | Transparent

(* Borders *)
type border_style = Solid | Dashed | Dotted | No_border
type border = { width : float; style : border_style; color : color; radius : float }

(* Shadow and the paint block *)
type overflow = Visible | Hidden
type shadow = { x : float; y : float; blur : float; spread : float; color : color }

type paint = {
  background : color option; border : border option; opacity : float;
  shadow : shadow option; overflow : overflow;
}
(* Style.default_shadow is zero offset, zero blur, zero spread, transparent.
   Style.default_paint is no background, no border, opacity 1.0, no shadow,
   Visible overflow — a default paint emits no CSS at all.

   shadow.spread grows the shadow outward on every side of the border box by
   that many pixels before the blur is applied; a negative spread contracts it.
   A shadow is painted and never laid out, so the focus-ring idiom
   { x = 0.; y = 0.; blur = 0.; spread = 3.; color = ... } placed in
   Interaction.focused draws a 3px ring around the control without moving it or
   anything after it — which a wider border on focus does not. A zero spread
   emits the same three-length declaration it emitted before spread was
   expressible, so existing shadows are unaffected. *)

(* Building styles *)
Style.default                                            (* sensible defaults *)
Style.with_layout : (layout -> layout) -> Style.t -> Style.t
Style.with_paint  : (paint -> paint)   -> Style.t -> Style.t
Style.with_text   : (Text.t -> Text.t) -> Style.t -> Style.t
Style.padding     : float -> float -> float -> float -> layout -> layout  (* T R B L, wraps in Some *)
Style.padding_all : float -> layout -> layout                             (* wraps in Some *)

Style.hex   : string -> color
Style.named : string -> color
Style.rgba  : int -> int -> int -> float -> color
```

### Interaction (`nopal_style`)

State-based style overrides for hover, press, and focus:

```ocaml
type Interaction.t = {
  hover   : Style.t option;
  pressed : Style.t option;
  focused : Style.t option;
}
(* The web backend emits these as .class:hover, .class:active and
   .class:focus-visible — focused is :focus-visible, not :focus, so a mouse
   click focuses the element without showing the style, by design. Rule order
   encodes precedence: hover, then focused, then pressed. *)
```

### Typography (`nopal_style`)

```ocaml
type Font.family = System_ui | Sans_serif | Serif | Monospace
                 | Ui_sans_serif | Ui_serif | Ui_monospace | Ui_rounded
                 | Custom of string   (* the name as written, never pre-quoted or pre-escaped *)
type Font.weight = Thin | Extra_light | Light | Normal | Medium | Semi_bold | Bold | Extra_bold | Black

(* The generics a stack may end in: the ones every target engine resolves to a
   real face. The Ui_* generics are not among them — Chromium renders each at
   the width of an unknown family, i.e. in its default face — so they may sit
   earlier in a stack (ui-monospace, monospace) but never last. *)
type Font.Generic.t = System_ui | Sans_serif | Serif | Monospace
Font.Generic.to_family : Font.Generic.t -> Font.family

type Font.stack                                     (* abstract *)
Font.stack : Font.family list -> last_resort:Font.Generic.t -> Font.stack
(* Families tried in order, then the required last resort. Omitting
   ~last_resort does not give a stack: a stack with no last resort is a type
   error. The list may be empty, giving the last resort alone. *)
Font.families     : Font.stack -> Font.family list  (* in order, last resort last; never empty *)
Font.equal_stack  : Font.stack -> Font.stack -> bool

Font.family_to_css_string : Font.family -> string
(* Generics are bare keywords (system-ui, sans-serif, serif, monospace,
   ui-sans-serif, ui-serif, ui-monospace, ui-rounded). A Custom name is
   double-quoted; inside the quotes " and \ are backslash-escaped, and { } ;
   and every control character (U+0000-U+001F, U+007F) are written as a
   lowercase CSS hex escape plus one space: Custom "a;b" gives "a\3b b". Every
   other character, spaces and commas included, is written as given, so a name
   is never read as a list, a keyword, a declaration or a rule boundary.
   Custom "serif" is a face called serif, not the Serif generic. An empty or
   whitespace-only name is serialised as written. This one serialiser feeds the
   CSS declaration, the canvas font shorthand and (XML-escaped) the SVG
   font-family attribute. *)
Font.stack_to_css_string : Font.stack -> string
(* Each family through family_to_css_string, joined by ", ":
   Font.stack [Custom "Geist"; System_ui] ~last_resort:Sans_serif
   gives "Geist", system-ui, sans-serif *)

type Text.font = Single of Font.family | Stack of Font.stack
(* Single is one family with no last resort: when that face is missing the
   engine falls back to its own default face, often a serif. Stack names what
   renders instead. *)

type Text.t = {
  font_family    : Text.font option;
  font_size      : float option;
  font_weight    : Font.weight option;
  line_height    : line_height option;     (* Lh_normal | Lh_multiplier f | Lh_px f *)
  letter_spacing : letter_spacing option;  (* Ls_normal | Ls_em f *)
  text_align     : text_align option;      (* Align_left | Align_center | Align_right | Align_justify *)
  text_decoration: text_decoration option; (* Underline | Line_through | Overline | No_decoration *)
  text_transform : text_transform option;  (* Uppercase | Lowercase | Capitalize | No_transform *)
  text_overflow  : text_overflow option;   (* Clip | Ellipsis | Wrap | No_wrap *)
  italic         : bool option;
  color          : Color.t option;         (* Rgba | Hex | Named | Transparent *)
  whitespace     : whitespace option;      (* Collapse | Preserve *)
  figure_spacing : figure_spacing option;  (* Tabular | Proportional | Normal_spacing *)
  figure_style   : figure_style option;    (* Lining | Oldstyle | Normal_style *)
  underline_offset : float option;         (* pixels *)
}

Text.font_family : Font.family -> Text.t -> Text.t   (* Some (Single f) *)
Text.font_stack  : Font.stack -> Text.t -> Text.t    (* Some (Stack s), replacing any single family *)
Text.equal_font  : Text.font -> Text.font -> bool    (* a Single never equals a Stack, even a one-entry one *)
(* The web backend emits either as one font-family declaration, with Font's
   bytes unchanged. To write 'Geist', system-ui, sans-serif:
   Text.font_stack (Font.stack [Custom "Geist"; System_ui] ~last_resort:Sans_serif)
   Font loading is not provided: a stack makes a fallback expressible, it does
   not make a web font available. *)

Text.underline_offset : float -> Text.t -> Text.t
(* Distance in pixels from the text to its underline; the web backend emits
   text-underline-offset:<n>px. A negative value is valid and emitted; a
   non-finite one (nan, infinity, neg_infinity) emits nothing, as if unset. It
   moves an underline only where one is drawn, at rest or in an interaction
   state, so a link gains an offset underline on hover with an interaction
   whose hover is Style.default |> Style.with_text (fun t ->
   t |> Text.text_decoration Text.Underline |> Text.underline_offset 3.0).
   Web-only: scene and canvas text draw no text
   decoration at all. *)

Text.color : Color.t -> Text.t -> Text.t
(* Text color, like every other field here, inherits only where the target
   platform cascades — the DOM backend does, a canvas or GPU backend does not.
   Portable authoring puts the color on the text element rather than on an
   ancestor box. The web backend emits it as the CSS color property. *)

Text.whitespace : whitespace -> Text.t -> Text.t
(* Whether runs of spaces and tabs in the content are significant — Preserve
   keeps them, so indented code keeps its indentation. Preserve also makes line
   breaks in the content significant: a newline renders as a break, because no
   platform value preserves spaces while collapsing newlines. This is only the
   collapsing axis; whether a line breaks stays with text_overflow's Wrap and
   No_wrap, and the two compose within one Text.t rather than override each
   other. The web backend folds the pair into a single white-space declaration
   emitted at most once: Preserve gives pre-wrap, or pre where the wrapping axis
   says no; unset or Collapse gives normal, or nowrap on the same condition;
   both axes unset emits nothing. Collapse is therefore not the same as None —
```
